title: Are our standards too high?
summary: A personal mailbag episode where both sisters, newly single, discuss their dating lives: dating apps versus friend setups, why they now avoid dating coworkers, and what they each want in a partner (Cherie: a funny, witty, fit nerd who challenges her; Jean: a slow-burn connection with someone she can learn from). They debate whether 'power couples' favor the man, and analyze the Bachelorette season with Jenn Tran as a case study in rose-colored glasses and 'I can fix him' thinking.

ideas.idea: A joyful, wealthy life needs a holistic approach; early-career focus on academic and professional achievement often comes at the cost of the personal department.
ideas.detail: The hosts say balancing work and dating is a real thing girlfriends talk about, and that is why they created the podcast to cover relationships alongside careers.

ideas.idea: A friend referral is a more serious and safer path to a partner than dating apps because the person is already vetted by someone who knows you both.
ideas.detail: Jean used dating apps until 2015 and is now hoping to meet people organically; Cherie notes she has never been set up and would love to be, while cautioning that a stranger's DM recommendation is risky.

ideas.idea: Meeting a stranger at a bar happens far less now because people are on their phones and have so many touch points on Instagram.
ideas.detail: Neither sister has ever dated a random person met while out; all of Jean's serious relationships came through school or work.

ideas.idea: After a date, ask whether you had fun because the other person was engaging or because you yourself are engaging.
ideas.detail: Cherie's girlfriends challenged her after a fun first date; Jean recalls dates with a car-collecting investment banker (Michelin restaurant, Scuderia) who was so boring she realized she was the entertainment.

ideas.idea: Playfulness and laughter should be a core tenet of a relationship, even at 50 or 60; someone who does not take themselves seriously is more fun.
ideas.detail: Cherie's last relationship felt like high school with constant giggling, a contrast to her past pattern of attractive but stoic partners; your partner is the number one person you talk to and build a life with, so they should be as fun as you.

ideas.idea: The question 'how do you balance work and dating' falsely implies they are separate buckets; for people working 40-100 hours a week they become one and the same.
ideas.detail: Proximity and repeated exposure build interest, which is why people end up dating coworkers.

ideas.idea: Do not date coworkers, especially on your immediate team; treat colleagues as a pool of people you could date after one of you leaves the company.
ideas.detail: Both have dated coworkers and it did not work out; seeing an ex in meetings every day is stressful. Jean's more positive relationships came from people she met through work but dated only a year or more later.

ideas.idea: Look for a partner who challenges you physically and intellectually and from whom you learn, in a relationship safe enough to admit you do not understand something.
ideas.detail: Cherie's ex, a strong snowboarder, took her down expert runs and coached her through; her last partner pushed her to understand economic markets without making her feel dumb because of mutual trust and respect.

ideas.idea: Know your own dating style: some people are slow-burn and date only after long platonic familiarity, others jump in fast.
ideas.detail: Jean says nearly everyone she dated seriously she had known and hung out with platonically for a month to years first; Cherie says she is the opposite.

ideas.idea: The power-couple ideal, two influential high-status people strategizing together, typically favors the man in heterosexual relationships because the woman steps back to invest in the family.
ideas.detail: Holding age, potential and performance constant, the woman usually takes the step back; the famous examples (Michelle and Barack Obama, Serena Williams and Alexis Ohanian) mostly became couples only after both reached career peaks.

ideas.idea: Someone who has survived trauma can get put on a pedestal so you read maturity into everything they do; beware the 'I can fix him' rose-colored glasses.
ideas.detail: Jean dated a man who beat cancer in college and assumed he was mature and thoughtful, missing red flags; she sees Bachelorette Jenn Tran doing the same with Army Ranger Marcus, who grew up in foster care and would need years of therapy she should not have to take on.

ideas.idea: Representation changes what gets discussed: the first Asian Bachelorette brought family trauma and self-confidence to a franchise historically white, Christian and traditional.
ideas.detail: Jenn Tran's openness about a father who abandoned her made the season deeper and more relatable than prior seasons centered on breakups and infidelity.

ideas.idea: Be honest about the gap between your 'old type' and the type you say you want; the ideal is the Venn diagram of dependable and playful.
ideas.detail: Cherie says she wants a funny, witty, fit nerd but her Bachelorette favorite is the stoic, sturdy Marcus, the same archetype as her exes; she realizes she likes responsible, dependable people but wants to evolve toward someone who is both.
